lesson.menu_title: The Language of Negotiation -- Reporting What Was Said and What Was Agreed
lesson.menu_desc: Agreed, proposed or rejected -- the verb that decides which -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- The Language of Negotiation
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Paula Teodoro Valdivia | Lesson 6 -- The Language of Negotiation
lesson.grammar_point: reporting verbs of negotiation and their patterns

listenings.text: Thirty years at the table, and almost none of my worst problems came from the table. They came from the summary somebody wrote afterwards. Here is how it happens. In the room, the other side says they are open to sixty days. Open to. By the time that reaches an email, it reads: they accepted sixty days. Nobody lied. Somebody just picked a stronger verb than the moment deserved, and nobody found it strange, because a summary always sounds confident. Three weeks later you are in a signing meeting, explaining why a term that nobody agreed to is sitting in the draft. So I gave my team a short list. Agreed, when the point is closed. Offered and proposed, when it is on the table. Refused and rejected, when it is dead. Insisted on, when they would not move. And I banned two words. Accepted, unless I can point at the moment they accepted it. And confirmed, which people use when they mean nothing more than nobody said no. Choose the verb first. The sentence writes itself after that.

I spend a large part of my week correcting three phrases that people treat as the same thing. Agreed means the point is closed: both sides said yes, and it goes into the contract. Agreed in principle means they like the direction and nothing more. It does not bind anybody, and it can disappear in the next round. And did not object means only that. Somebody made a proposal, the other side said nothing, and silence is not a yes. I learned that from a file I still think about. Our summary said the counterparty had accepted the indexation clause. What actually happened in the meeting was that the counterparty said nothing when it was mentioned. Six weeks and a lot of money later, they told us they had never agreed to it, and they were right. So now I write every summary the same way. Each line starts with a verb, and I choose the verb before I write the sentence. Agreed, proposed, offered, refused, did not respond. If I cannot pick one of them honestly, the line is not ready to send.

extra_audio.text: They agreed to extend the term by sixty days. They proposed a five percent cap, but nothing is signed. They refused to discuss exclusivity, so that point is in deadlock. I would send a counteroffer before the next round.
